entries.title: Iran: Exiled journalists still repressed by regime
entries.summary: For many independent reporters, leaving Iran does not mean fully escaping the grasp of the Iranian state. The regime uses family members, bank accounts and the property they left behind to apply pressure across borders.
entries.content:
November 12, 2026

For many independent reporters, leaving Iran does not mean fully escaping the grasp of the Iranian state. The regime uses family members, bank accounts and the property they left behind to apply pressure across borders.

In times of crisis, Iran's political system is looking for scapegoats — and independent journalists, even journalists who have been living in exile for a long time, are high on their list.

At the end of September, Iran's judiciary announced that it had confiscated assets belonging to individuals accused of "cooperation with hostile governments." The measure is part of a previously announced plan targeting around 400 people living abroad, including journalists, activists, artists and athletes, whose assets are to be seized.

"The only thing I own in my parents' house in Iran is a bookshelf," says Amir Soltanzadeh. The exiled freelance journalist, who occasionally works for Germany's international broadcaster DW, discovered his name on a government list, which Iranian state media had labeled "traitors to the homeland." His assets were to be seized. In an online post earlier this year, he published a photo of his book collection and wrote: "This library is my only asset in Iran. If you enjoy reading books, go ahead and confiscate them."

'My father lost his job because of me'

Soltanzadeh said that his bank account in Iran was also frozen. It contained the equivalent of around €500 ($555), which he used, among other things, to buy his family members gifts and flowers for special occasions. He noted it was "unjust" to list him as a traitor.

"I have not acted against Iran," he stressed. "Every position I have taken was ultimately aimed at improving the lives of people in Iran."

Some of his relatives, he said, have cut ties with his family because of his journalistic work.

"When people hear about a journalist working abroad, some who adopt the government's narrative automatically equate that person with a spy. They see a journalist as someone who is paid to gather information," said Soltanzadeh.

This pressure, according to the exiled journalist, eventually extended to his father's workplace.

"My father lost his job because of me. And because of me, my mother lives in constant anxiety — every time the phone rings, she has to wonder who is on the other end."

For several months, Soltanzadeh also cut all direct contact with his family to keep them safe, and only communicated with them through an intermediary.

Regime using vague laws to control media reporting

Pressure against independent journalists is a part of a recurring pattern in the Islamic Republic. In times of political tension, Western media outlets and journalists are often portrayed as agents of hostile intelligence services such as the CIA or Mossad, or mouthpieces spreading subversive propaganda.

The authorities have many tools to spy on reporters, including hacking their social media accounts and intercepting conversations that are later used as evidence against their contacts inside Iran.

Such forms of repression also affect which information ends up reaching the public.

A journalist in Iran, who wanted to stay anonymous, says that reporting on detainees, state executions and the treatment of protesters comes with major risks and restrictions.

"Journalists can only write on their personal pages in a very limited and censored way," the reporter said. "In their reports, they are required to follow the government's official narrative."

Iran-based journalists have to weigh potential legal consequences of their work. This, in turn, constrains their ability to conduct independent research, maintain contact with sources and pursue sensitive topics.

Article 24 of Iran's constitution guarantees freedom of the press. However, the Press Law has been amended and expanded several times over the past four decades. It requires media professionals, among other things, not to endanger the Islamic Republic, not to insult the clergy or the Supreme Leader, and not to disseminate false information. These broadly worded provisions give authorities significant room to interfere in the work of the media.

Danger follows reporters abroad

Many journalists are forced to leave the country due to the constant pressure and the risk of being targeted by the authorities.

"Because of my journalistic work, I had to go into exile," says Omid Barin, a freelance journalist who also occasionally contributes to DW.

Barin's reporting focuses on issues such as human rights violations and the position of ethnic minorities in Iran. The pressure "has undoubtedly caused me to be much more cautious and sensitive when communicating with sources inside the country, to avoid putting them in danger," he told DW.

While Barin chooses not to provide details on the threats he faces, citing the risk of backlash on the people close to him, he says the core message behind them is clear: Someone in Iran would like him to either abandon journalism or steer away from sensitive topics.

Even while living abroad, Barin is forced to take additional precautions in his daily life and pay close attention to his personal security due to his work for media outlets that the Iranian regime considers "hostile."

entries.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as scandal mounts over alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy
entries.summary: Jensen Huang has resigned from his role as the head of the AI chipmaker over his reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
entries.content:
United States of America

Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO

November 12, 2026

Jensen Huang has resigned from his role as the head of the AI chipmaker over his reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang has resigned from his role as the head of the AI chipmaker Nvidia over his reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the company said in a statement on Thursday.

Colette Kress, the company's current executive vice president and chief financial officer, has been named as interim CEO.

"Nvidia's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said in a statement.

Why did Jensen Huang resign?

Huang resigned after facing growing calls to step down over his reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia had been investigating whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after reports of an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

In an email to Nvidia staff, Huang said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who worked for him.

Shares in Nvidia, one of the world's biggest companies, plummeted 13% at the opening of trading on Thursday.

The latest declines mean Nvidia has now lost about $800 billion (€721.4 bln) since the reports of the affair with the suspected Chinese spy came to light.

Who is Jensen Huang?

Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia, which he led for more than three decades, turning it from a gaming chipmaker into the dominant supplier of chips for artificial intelligence.

This a developing news story, more to follow...

entries.title: China's Xi Jinping renews calls for 'reunification' with Taiwan
entries.summary: Xi Jinping said that reunification was inevitable, but stopped short of mentioning military force. Taiwan though swiftly rejected Beijing's demands as tensions continue over the island's future.
entries.content:
China

China's Xi Jinping renews calls for 'reunification' with Taiwan

November 12, 2026

Xi Jinping said that reunification was inevitable, but stopped short of mentioning military force. Taiwan though swiftly rejected Beijing's demands as tensions continue over the island's future.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has renewed his calls for "reunification” with Taiwanbut refrained from mentioning the use of force.

"The historical trends are unstoppable. The complete reunification of our motherland must be realized, and it can, without doubt, be realized," Xi said on Thursday.

His comments came in a speech marking the 160th birthday of Sun Yat-sen, the political leader who helped lead the 1911 revolution that overthrew China's imperial dynasty and led to the founding the Republic of China.

The Taiwanese government swiftly rebuffed the remarks, saying the territory would not accept submitting to the rule of China's Communist Party.

What is the Taiwan conflict about?

After the founding of the Republic of China in 1912, a civil war broke out in 1927 between the Nationalists and the Communists.

After the end of Japanese occupation and World War II, the Communists led by Mao Zedong gained the upper hand and the Nationalists retreated to the island of Taiwan in 1949.

Since then, both the People's Republic of China on the mainland and the Republic of China in Taiwan claim to be the legitimate heirs of Sun Yat-sen's political legacy.

Under the so-called One China policy, the majority of the international community recognizes only Communist China on the mainland as a state. Many countries nevertheless also maintain unofficial diplomatic, economic and cultural ties with Taiwan, which is self-governed and democratic.

What did Xi say about reunification?

While the speech by the Chinese president was largely about commemorating Sun Yat-sen, it was his remarks about Taiwan that drew international attention.

Xi said that reunification was an unwavering historical mission for the Communist Party and that "we will never leave any room for ‘Taiwan independence' separatist activities in any form.”

"We will definitely give full consideration to Taiwan's realities and take full account of the interests and feelings of our compatriots in Taiwan.

"Mr. Sun Yat-sen consistently upheld the unity of the country and the solidarity of the nation, and he firmly opposed all words and actions that split the country or the nation," he added.

While not mentioning military force in his speech, the Chinese leader has on several occasions in the past said that Beijing would not rule out military force to bring Taiwan under its control.

In response to Xi's speech on Thursday, Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council reiterated that neither the government nor the people of Taiwan would accept being placed under Beijing's rule.

"As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn't much different from ​the past," council spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told reporters.

Increased pressure on Taiwan

Xi Jinping's speech came ahead on an APEC summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen where the Chinese leader is expected to meet with US President Donald Trump.

The US has over the past decades been backing Taiwan's resistance against Chinese demands, supplying the island with vital arms support.

China has in past years intensified its military operations around the island and in the Taiwan Strait, widely seen as both attempts to intimidate Taipei and to possibly practice for an eventual military operation.

On Thursday, Taiwan said that Chinese fighter jets and drones had begun carrying out a "joint combat readiness patrol" alongside Chinese warships around the island.

entries.title: What are fossil fuels?
entries.summary: They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

What are fossil fuels?

November 12, 2026

They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

What exactly are fossil fuels?

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen. 

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others. 

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

How are fossil fuels used?

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950. 

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport. 

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas. 

What is the future of fossil fuels?

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise. 

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent. 

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise. 

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

entries.title: Israel strikes Gaza hospital, says Hamas senior figure inside
entries.summary: Israel says Hamas was using the hospital as a military command center, while Palestinian officials report at least six people killed, including a surgeon. The strike comes amid an increasingly fragile ceasefire.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel strikes Gaza hospital, says Hamas senior figure inside

November 12, 2026

Israel says Hamas was using the hospital as a military command center, while Palestinian officials report at least six people killed, including a surgeon. The strike comes amid an increasingly fragile ceasefire.

Israel said it had targeted a senior Hamas member in a Gaza  hospital in an overnight airstrike which reportedly killed six people.

According to the Israeli military, Muhammad Abu Ismail and other militants from the Islamist group had been operating a command center inside the Nasser hospital in Khan Yunis.

Gaza's civil defense service said at least six people were killed, including a surgeon and more than 20 were wounded. It said that parts of several floors were severely damaged or destroyed.

During war, hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law, although they can lose that protection if they are used for military purposes.

Israel says hospital used for terrorist activities

In a statement on Thursday, the Israeli military (IDF) said, without providing evidence, that Hamas was "operating within Nasser Hospital in Khan Yunis" and were using the complex "as a hub for military and terrorist activities against IDF troops and Israel."

The IDF identified the targeted senior Hamas member as Abu Ismail, adding he "was responsible for directing terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops and for holding numerous hostages captive throughout the war."

The IDF said the hospital was used for storing weapons, to conduct interrogation, operate command-and-control rooms as well as to shelter terrorists.

What happened at the hospital?

The Gaza Health Ministry said the Israeli airstrike hit the surgery department, killing six people including surgeon Rizk Abu Sharia.

News agency Reuters reported seeing footage from inside the hospital showing extensive damage with debris scattered around rooms and equipment.

Wounded people were also seen in the wreckage while several bodies were being carried away as firefighters worked to clear the scene.

Hamas has described the strike as a "fully-fledged war crime."

Since the beginning of the war in 2023, Israeli forces have attacked several hospitals in the Gaza Strip.

Fragile ceasefire

The war on Hamas in Gaza began in October 2023 after Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

Since then, more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.

More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel's war in the enclave.

A ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, but attacks have continued since then. While Israel says Hamas is trying to regroup, the Palestinian militant group says it's committed to the ceasefire and that Israel is trying to undermine the agreement.

Hamas is recognized as a terrorist organization by the EU, the US and several Arab states.

entries.title: Germany news: Police raid chapters of Gremium MC biker gang
entries.summary: Police in southwestern Germany launched major early-morning operations against a biker gang. The state of Baden-Württemberg is outlawing three of its chapters. Meanwhile, unions are planning more strikes. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Police raid chapters of Gremium MC biker gang

Published November 12, 2026last updated November 12, 2026

Police in southwestern Germany launched major early-morning operations against a biker gang. The state of Baden-Württemberg is outlawing three of its chapters. Meanwhile, unions are planning more strikes. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police raid sites tied to the Gremium MC biker gang in Baden-Württemberg
  • The IG Metall union is expected to announce more strikes in the carmaking and metwalworking sectors
  • The Bundestag budget committee is discussing outstanding 2027 spending issues, a day after the coalition walked back some banner economic reforms
  • Earliest Christmas markets start to open, with Glühwein/mulled wine typically costing almost €5 per cup
  • 1 in 10 Germans showing signs of being in excessive debt
  • German DAX index clears 27,000 points for first time

Here's a roundup of news from or pertaining to Germany on November 12, 2026:

Skip next section IG Metall union paves way for 1-day warning strikes in metalworking, electronics

IG Metall union paves way for 1-day warning strikes in metalworking, electronics

Germany's major IG Metall trade union has enabled the possibility of longer warning strikes amid difficult negotiations for industrial employees.

"The board of IG Metall has pave the way for 24-hour warning strikes in the metalworking and electrical industry," the union said on Thursday.

The union accuses employers of intransigence after three rounds of negotiations without clear progress.

On Wednesday, regional chapters appealed for authorization for full-day warning strikes — the last step before a full union vote and an indefinite labor dispute.

"This escalation is completely excessive and counterproductive," Udo Dinglreiter, the president of the employers' umbrella organization, Gesamtmetall, said. He said that hundreds of thousands of jobs could be at risk.

IG Metall's first chairperson Christiane Benner countered that "the employers want to turn this round of collective bargaining into a dispute over principles." Another union official said they were offering what amounted to a real-terms pay cut rather than seeking solutions.

IG Metall is calling for a 5% pay increase and other improved conditions for some 3.7 million workers starting in November, while employers have offered a one-off payment in 2027 coupled with a 1.3% increase starting in the summer of 2028.

The union estimates that around 464,000 employees took part in the initial wave of warning strikes that were limited to periods of hours, rather than full days.

Employers argue that they're treading a difficult line between trying not to cut jobs and meeting calls for improved pay amid widespread industrial sector layoffs in Germany in recent years.

Skip next section Mulled wine prices rising, but roughly in line with inflation, as Christmas markets open

Mulled wine prices rising, but roughly in line with inflation, as Christmas markets open

'Tis the season, already. Preparations are underway around Germany and in several cities, Christmas markets are opening to the public.

Some markets are already open in Essen and in Hamburg, Duisburg's opens on Thursday, and Cologne's follows a day later. 

The coupons.de website has sought to track the planned prices for mulled wine or Glühwein as the markets open their doors nationwide.

The bad news? These prices are rising like so many others. The better news? The year-on-year increase is actually smaller than overall inflation figures, at around 1%.

On average, a cup is liable to set you back around €4.60 (roughly $5.10). Not entirely surprisingly, Munich tops the nationwide pricing chart, with the price peaking at €7. Other sites nationwide tend not to have the gall even to charge 6 euros.

Bargain hunters determined to get the best value mulled wine will need to venture deep into the center of Germany — hardly its core tourist hub — to find the lowest prices starting at around €3.50.

Deposits for the cup, the "Pfand," are also only going in one direction, and in the meantime range from €1 all the way up to €5. But there's a strong argument, particularly with the better designs or after a memorable trip, that this can be money well spent as a memento!

Skip next section Sauna fire in northwest causes major damage to building complex

Sauna fire in northwest causes major damage to building complex

Police in the Emsland region in the northwest near the border to the Netherlands have reported a major fire in a complex of residential and commercial buildings in Papenburg.

The fire broke out on Wednesday afternoon, police said the following morning, causing damages worth "at least €10 million ($11 million)." Several hundred emergency services personnel were deployed.

"Based on current findings, the fire broke out in the sauna area of a gym facility on site, and quickly spread to further parts of the complex of buildings," police wrote.

Two men were in the sauna at the time and initially tried to douse the flames but without success.

Police said the buildings were evacuated as the fire spread, with some surrounding buildings also being cleared as a precaution because of possible smoke-related dangers.

Several people were injured, police said, including the two men in the sauna area suffering mild burns and suspected smoke inhalation sickness. They were treated in a nearby hospital but soon discharged.

"There were also injuries among the first responders," police wrote. "Four police officers, two firefighters and members of the rescue teams suffered mild injuries, particularly via smoke inhalation."

The fire was only extinguished late on Wednesday night, several hours after it started. The area is sealed off, with possible risks of damaged buildings collapsing. Police have also launched investigations into the fire's cause, but said that at present, the area was not safe for that work to start at full scale.

Skip next section Study: 1 in 10 German residents show signs of excessive debt

Study: 1 in 10 German residents show signs of excessive debt

Germany's largest credit bureau Creditreform has published its "2026 Debtors' Atlas." 

It finds that 10.16% of German adults, or 7.36 million people, exhibit at least the early warning signs of excessive debt. A year ago the ratio was 9.74%.

"The financial situation of private consumers has further deteriorated," Patrik-Ludwig Hantzsch, Creditreform's head of economic research, said. "In particular, the sharply increased living costs, energy costs and housing costs are straining expenditures."

Hantzsch said employment was also becoming an issue once more, saying "above all, well-paid jobs in manufacturing industries have been cut back in large numbers in recent months."

The report also highlights rising cases of signs of excessive debt prior to legal action being taken, such as payment reminders or warnings being sent, saying "consumers are taking on more credit-financed expenditures — increasingly also for smaller purchases — at simultaneously rising interest rates."

A larger share of men than women have excessive debts, perpetuating a longstanding trend.

People around the middle of their working lives, aged 30-39 and 40-49, are most likely to be affected — but the cohort with the fastest-rising share of people with excessive debts are young adults below the age of 30.

Bremen, Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt and North Rhine-Westphalia were among the states with the highest rates of excess debts, while the wealthy and fiscally conservative states of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg had the lowest levels.

Skip next section DAX clears 27,000 points for first time

DAX clears 27,000 points for first time

Germany's main DAX stock market index has cleared the 27,000-point mark for the first time in its history in morning trading. 

It climbed by around 1.3% in order to pass the milestone.

A combination of some positive outlook data from major companies, not least engineering giant Siemens, and the falling oil prices of recent days have helped fuel the uptick. 

Siemens' shares had risen by almost 5%, to just over €291 (around $323) each, helping to spur on the gains and making the company the morning's top performer.

Despite several years of low growth and recession in the German economy, the DAX, like many Western indices, is now trading twice as high as it was prior to the COVID pandemic.

Skip next section Police raid sites of Gremium MC biker gang in Baden-Württemberg

Police raid sites of Gremium MC biker gang in Baden-Württemberg

Hundreds of police officers searched apartments and meeting sites for the biker group "Gremium MC" in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg early on Thursday. 

The state interior ministry said the operation was part of a move to outlaw three sub-chapters of the group, the ones based in Böblingen and Leonberg, as well as the "Gremium MC Chapter Nomads Bosphorus Türkiye."

This last group was highlighted as a meaningful part of Gremium MC by security officials. It describes itself on Facebook as a great example that "people of different cultures and faiths can be strong together," featuring images of men posing with knives and other weapons.

Gremium MC prominently incorporates into its iconography the symbol of the Prussian military medal for exceptional valor, the Iron Cross, which was discontinued after World War I, reintroduced by Adolf Hitler during World War II, and then scrapped for good.

State Interior Minister Manuel Hagel was expected to make further comments later in the day in Ludwigsburg.

Gremium MC is deemed an "outlaw motorcycle gang" in Baden-Württemberg's latest security report, a term used for biker groups that do not recognize the state monopoly on the use of force and are often tied to organized crime.

"Extortion, drug dealing and pimping in particular tend to be part of their activities," state authorities say.

Baden-Württemberg counts 154 biker chapters in the state with around 2,000 members.

Founded in 1972 in Mannheim, various chapters of Gremium MC across the country have faced legal issues in recent years. In 2021, another chapter in the southwest, Gremium MC Southgate in Heidelberg, was outlawed on suspicion of organized crime activity.

Skip next section Hanover: 3 injured by attacker in car overnight

Hanover: 3 injured by attacker in car overnight

Police in Hanover reported early on Thursday that three men were injured by an unknown driver in a car in the nearby town of Ronneberg.

One person sustained severe injuries in the incident late on Wednesday, police said.

Two of the wounded were taken to a nearby hospital while the other could be cared for at the scene.

Police said the driver fled the scene and that a search operation was ongoing. Authorities were also still investigating a potential motive for the apparent attack.

Skip next section Welcome to our updates

Welcome to our updates

Gemorsche and/or Gudde Morga!

Today's updates start with a focus between the southwestern Kurpfalz and Swabian regions, where police have launched major morning raids against a biker gang.

The state Interior Ministry in Baden Württemberg has outlawed three of its chapters. Hundreds of police officers mobilized in the early hours of the morning. 

The major IG Metall trade union is planning further strikes in the carmaking sector and other metalworking industries, with an announcement anticipated later in the day. 

To the north, near Hanover, police report an apparent car attack injuring three men overnight.

And in the spirit of offering the public service journalism people are truly thirsting for, we'll have some info on the average and localized pricing of mulled wine or Glühwein at Christmas markets this year, as the early birds start to open their doors to visitors. (Yes, already!)

Stay tuned for updates on all this and anything else of note in or pertaining to Germany as the day progresses.

entries.title: Australian teen found alive after six days in the bush
entries.summary: The teenager was spotted during an aerial search, after spending days navigating rugged terrain. He had fallen down the side of a riverbed two days before being found.
entries.content:
November 12, 2026

The teenager was spotted during an aerial search, after spending days navigating rugged terrain. He had fallen down the side of a riverbed two days before being found.

An Australianteenager has been found alive after six days missing in dense bushland. 

Police said 17-year-old William had been camping with a friend in the southeastern state of Victoria, about 180 kilometers (112 miles) east of Melbourne. He got lost after he'd left his friend to go and get some equipment, but didn't return.

The friend then called the police and an intense search operation was launched, involving helicopters, special units, as well as volunteers searching the bush each day.

The boy was found on Thursday morning during an aerial search near Stoney Creek, public broadcaster ABC reported. Rescuers first spotted a fishing tackle box and then saw the boy sleeping on a rock in a dry riverbed.

'In good spirits and good health'

Pictures show the boy shirtless and sunburned. Local media reported that he waved and pumped his fist when he was woken up the sound of the search helicopter.

"Flight officers winched down and retrieved Will before bringing him back to the command post to reunite with his mum," police said. "Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health."

He was then taken to hospital for monitoring.

"I'm just over the moon he's alive," his mother was quoted in Australian media. "He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued."

Police said William had spent days walking through the rugged terrain but fell down the side of a riverbed two days ago and then remained there in hopes of being found.

"He's never leaving the house again," his mother told local reporters. "He's grounded for life."

entries.title: Bundeswehr study exposes widespread sexual harassment in German military
entries.summary: Sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known, with younger women disproportionately affected. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has called for a policy of "zero tolerance."
entries.content:
Germany

Bundeswehr study exposes sexual harassment in German military

November 12, 2026

Sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known, with younger women disproportionately affected. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has called for a policy of "zero tolerance."

"It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, on Wednesday.

Earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defense Committee. According to the findings, sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known.

"The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius said, announcing an action plan to address the issue.

"There is zero tolerance for sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr. This is nothing less than a matter of upholding the human dignity enshrined in our Basic Law. And that principle applies all the more within the Bundeswehr."

What the Bundeswehr study found

The study examined incidents that had gone unreported, the so-called "dark figure" of cases that never reach official statistics. The Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences (ZMSBw) surveyed 45,000 service members, around 18% of whom responded. More than 8,100 questionnaires were evaluated and supplemented with individual and group interviews. According to the institute, the data are statistically representative.

According to the study, younger women in the lower ranks are particularly affected by sexual misconduct. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. The perpetrators are predominantly male. Statistically, combat units do not differ from the rest of the armed forces.

Female service members in units with a higher proportion of women (more than 15%) are less likely to be affected.

Verbal harassment is by far the most common form of misconduct, according to the study. Around 72% of female soldiers and 31% of male soldiers said they had experienced verbal harassment at least once during their military service. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 38% of female soldiers and 16% of male soldiers reported experiencing verbal sexual harassment.

For physical harassment, 9% of female soldiers and 3% of male soldiers reported incidents of physical sexual misconduct, and 2% of both women and men said they had experienced sexual violence.

The study also examined why service members chose not to report incidents. The most commonly cited reason was not wanting to draw attention to themselves.

"There appears to be a lack of awareness of the reporting channels. And, for me, the decisive issue is trust in those channels," Pistorius concluded.

Greens call for independent reporting office for victims

In response, the Bundeswehr plans to improve awareness of how and where cases of sexual harassment can be reported. That is precisely where the environmentalist Greens, who are in opposition in the Bundestag, direct their criticism.

Defense policy spokesperson Sara Nanni is calling for "an external reporting office, alongside the regular disciplinary process, with investigative powers and the authority to take disciplinary action where appropriate." Such an independent point of contact, she argues, is needed in cases where superiors within the Bundeswehr fail to fulfill their responsibilities.

Another consequence of the study is the expansion of support services for those affected. A counseling center established in early November will soon be available around the clock. Supervisors are also to receive enhanced awareness training and improved instruction.

"Sexual misconduct will become part of training at every level, from the very beginning," said Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer.

In addition, the way supervisors handle reported cases will become a standing criterion in their performance evaluations. "Anyone who fails to lead by example, tolerates misconduct, or does not address it consistently will no longer hold a leadership position," Defense Minister Pistorius stressed.

Reported cases of sexual misconduct on the rise

The study was prompted by a growing number of reports of sexual misconduct received by former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces Eva Högl. Most of those who approached her were female soldiers. Högl called for the study into unreported cases in 2024. The process gained further momentum following incidents at the Parachute Regiment in Zweibrücken that came to light at the beginning of this year and also involved allegations of sexual misconduct.

The current Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, Henning Otte, described the figures revealed by the study as "dramatically high." The findings had also made it clear, he said, "that there is a lack of trust in the Bundeswehr's structures. The Ministry of Defense must now take this study seriously and translate its findings into a leadership culture that is truly lived in practice."

The Bundeswehr urgently needs additional personnel and has been actively recruiting women. However, the study's findings are unlikely to make attracting more female recruits any easier. Women remain significantly underrepresented across nearly all branches of the armed forces.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds
entries.summary: Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Women who score high on intelligence tests get less help at work

November 12, 2026

Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

Why are intelligent women seen as hostile at work?

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

Do men with high intelligence scores face the same treatment?

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

Should women hide their intelligence at work?

No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

What can managers do about gender bias at work?

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

entries.title: India news : Modi government approves $340 million museum in Delhi
entries.summary: The government says that the 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' will have the world's "largest" museum dispaly area." DW has the latest.
entries.content:
India

India news : Modi government approves $340 million museum in Delhi

Published November 12, 2026last updated November 12, 2026

The government says that the 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' will have the world's "largest" museum dispaly area." DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India's cabinet has passed plans to develop the 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' showcasing India's civilization journey
  • Two colonial-era blocks in Central Delhi, that earlier as government offices, are being transformed to house the museum
  • The first gallery under the project is expected to open next year

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of headlines from India on Thursday, November 12:

Skip next section 2 missing police officers found dead in India-administered Kashmir's Kishtwar

2 missing police officers found dead in India-administered Kashmir's Kishtwar

The bodies of two special police officers were recovered in Jammu and Kashmir's Kishtwar district on Thursday, Indian media reported.

Indian media said the pair were deployed with the Special Operations Group (SOG) of the local police in the remote Kiyar village.

They had reportedly gone missing on Wednesday while traveling from their camp to an army camp in the Dharna-Marwah area.

The officers' bodies were found riddled with bullets and their service weapons were missing. Police sources suggested this could indicate a possible militant angle.

"One body was found around 8 a.m., and the second was recovered around 9 a.m. It is deeply tragic," Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) Shagun Parihar, who represents the Kishtwar Assembly constituency, told news agency ANI.

In a separate incident on Wednesday, three personnel of the paramilitary Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) were injured in South Kashmir's Kulgam when suspected militants opened fire on a security checkpoint.

Kashmir, a disputed territory between India and Pakistan, has witnessed a decades-long insurgency. 

Mallikarjun Kharge, the president of India's main opposition Congress party, on Thursday addressed the Kishtwar and Kulgam incidents and said that India stood "united and resolute against terrorism."

Skip next section Man dies in paragliding accident in Bir Billing

Man dies in paragliding accident in Bir Billing

A tourist has reportedly died after falling from a paraglider in Bir Billing, known as India's paragliding capital, Indian media has reported.

The incident has raised concerns over the safety of commercial skydiving ventures in the popular adventure tourism spot located in the Kangra district of the Himalayan state of Himachal Pradesh.

Reports said the accident took place on Tuesday evening and identified the deceased tourist as a 26-year-old man from Uttar Pradesh's Noida.

News agency PTI cited police as saying the man had been on a tandem paragliding flight with a local pilot. He reportedly fell just six minutes after take-off.

The police have registered a case of death due to negligence against the pilot adding that a further probe into the incident was underway.

This is the second paragliding death to be reported in the densely forested and mountainous district in less than a month.

On October 25, a 47-year-old Bulgarian national was killed in a paraglider crash near Rising Star Peak in Kangra district's Dharamshala.

Skip next section Mega museum on Indian civilization gets cabinet nod

Mega museum on Indian civilization gets cabinet nod

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has approved the development of a massive museum in the heart of India's capital, New Delhi, estimated to cost around $340 million (around €306 million).

The 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' — which was first announced by Modi in 2023 — is being billed as the museum "with the largest display area in the world."

The Sanskrit name of the museum translates to 'India through the ages'. The project has been envisaged as the country's landmark museum, the government said, and will showcase elements of Indian history and civilization, which spans thousands of years.

Modi hails 'timeless richness' of Indian civilization

The century-old North and South Blocks in New Delhi's Raisina Hills — the seat of the Indian government — will be reused for the museum.

The colonial-era twin blocks once housed government offices, including Modi's own, before they were vacated over the last year as part of the Modi government's redesigning of India's hub of political power. 

The Hindu nationalist government has long sought to emphasize India's pre-colonial cultural identity.

"Buildings that have been centres of governance will now become a place where millions can discover, experience and celebrate the timeless richness of our civilisation," Modi wrote on X on Wednesday night.

Calling the museum a "magnificent celebration" of India's "civilizational journey", Modi said the museum's galleries will bring to life aspects including ancient knowledge systems, mathematics, astronomy to architecture, art, languages and spirituality, through "immersive experiences."

Inaugural gallery to open in 2027

According to a press release from the Indian cabinet, the museum will encompass an area of nearly 178,509 square meters with the ability to welcome some 10 million visitors a year. 

The finalization of the project isn't planned until 2030/31, but the first gallery on the theme of "adornment" will open its doors to the public next year, with more galleries gradually opening after that.

The content and collection analysis for the museum is currently underway, with the government having identified some 1.8 million objects for possible display from national and state museums, alongside archaeological and private collections.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Thursday wrap of all the biggest headlines from India.

Delhi's skyline is once again shrouded in a gray haze as the Indian capital's smog woes continue.

Nevertheless, India's cabinet has greenlit a multimillion‑dollar project to develop a mega-museum exhibiting aspects of India's civilizational history in the heart of the country's corridor of political power. It is touted to be the museum with the largest display area in the world.

Stay tuned to find out what India is talking about today.
